questions.prompt: A system bus is usually described as three buses. Which?
options: Input, output and control
Read, write and clock
Address, data and control
Internal, external and expansion
questions.explanation: The address bus says where, the data bus carries what, and the control bus says when and in which direction.

questions.prompt: What does the width of the address bus determine?
options: How fast memory can be read
How many devices can interrupt
How many bits each transfer carries
How much memory can be addressed
questions.explanation: An n-bit address bus can name 2^n locations. The data bus width is what decides how many bits move per transfer - a different question.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of interrupt-driven I/O over polling?
options: The CPU does useful work instead of asking the device repeatedly
It transfers data faster once started
It needs no device driver
It cannot be interrupted by other devices
questions.explanation: Polling burns cycles asking a device that is usually not ready. With interrupts the device speaks when it has something to say, and the CPU is free until then.

questions.prompt: What must be saved before the CPU jumps to an interrupt handler?
options: The whole of main memory
The program counter and the processor status, at minimum
Only the accumulator
Nothing: the handler starts from scratch
questions.explanation: The interrupted program must resume as if nothing happened, so the return address and the flags are pushed first. Anything else the handler modifies it must save and restore itself.

questions.prompt: Why does DMA exist when interrupt-driven I/O already frees the CPU from waiting?
options: Because interrupts are unreliable
Because DMA is faster than the bus
Because the CPU still copies every word by hand under interrupt-driven I/O
Because interrupts cannot be used with disks
questions.explanation: Interrupt-driven I/O frees the CPU from waiting, not from working: it still executes an instruction per word transferred. DMA hands the whole block to a controller that moves it over the bus directly, and interrupts the CPU once at the end.

questions.prompt: A non-maskable interrupt arrives while the CPU is executing an instruction with interrupts disabled. What happens?
options: It is ignored, like any other interrupt
It is queued until interrupts are enabled again
It causes the processor to reset
It is serviced anyway: that is what non-maskable means
questions.explanation: Maskable interrupts can be switched off; a non-maskable one cannot, because it signals something that cannot wait - power failure, a memory parity error. It still waits for the current instruction to finish, but the disable flag does not apply to it.
